speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. Today we're talking about GitHub Actions, which is GitHub's built-in automation system for repositories.

speaker: JAMIE
text: This is the thing that suddenly starts running when you open a pull request, right? Tests, checks, little status icons, sometimes a red X that makes everyone nervous.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Actions are event-driven automation. Something happens in the repository, like a commit being pushed or a pull request being opened, and GitHub runs a workflow that the maintainers defined.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So as a contributor, I may not be writing the automation, but I still need to understand what it is telling me.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Most contributors only need to read the results, follow the links when something fails, and make a focused fix. The written appendix is also a reference, so you can jump to the part you need later instead of memorizing every possible workflow feature today.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's slow down on the vocabulary, because Actions has a lot of nested words. Workflow, job, step, action, runner... they all sound similar at first.

speaker: ALEX
text: A workflow is the full automated process, and it is stored in a YAML file. YAML is a plain text format where indentation matters, so spaces at the start of a line change what belongs under what.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And a job is inside the workflow?

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. A job is a group of steps that run together, usually on one machine. A step might run a command, like npm test, or use a reusable action, like actions/checkout, which downloads the repository code into the runner.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Runner is the machine doing the work?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. GitHub-hosted runners are virtual machines such as ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or macos-latest. The workflow says which runner to use with the key runs-on.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where do I find these workflow files if I'm browsing a repository?

speaker: ALEX
text: They live in a required folder path:.github/workflows. The folder name starts with a dot, so a screen reader may announce it as "dot github." On GitHub.com, the file browser shows it, and you can press T to open Go to file and search for workflow YAML files, usually ending in.yml.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What would I actually hear or read inside a simple workflow file?

speaker: ALEX
text: A common file might be called.github/workflows/ci.yml. Near the top, name: CI gives the workflow its display name. Then on: defines the events that start it, jobs: lists the work to do, and steps: lists the individual commands or reusable actions.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So if I hear on colon, then pull_request under it, that's saying this workflow runs when a pull request changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Other common triggers are push, schedule, workflow_dispatch, release, issue_comment, pull_request_review, and merge_group. Schedule means a timer, workflow_dispatch means someone can start it manually from the Actions tab, and pull_request is the one contributors usually notice first.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Because that is the one that runs checks on my PR.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. On the pull request Conversation tab, near the merge area, GitHub shows status checks. A yellow or orange spinner means the check is still running, a green checkmark means it passed, a red X means something failed, and a gray slashed circle usually means the check was skipped by design.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And required checks are the ones that can block merging.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Non-required checks may still be useful, but required checks must pass before the pull request can be merged, if the repository has that rule enabled. Some projects also put status badges in the README so visitors can see whether the main branch is currently passing its workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I'm using NVDA or JAWS, how do I get to the checks without wandering the whole page?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open the pull request Conversation tab, then move by headings with H, or by heading level if that is easier, until you find the checks area. Each result is usually exposed as a link or button with a name and status, and you can press Enter on a failed one to open more detail.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And with VoiceOver on macOS?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use VO+U to open the Rotor, choose Headings, move to the checks area, then read through the results with VO+Arrow. When you find the failed check link, activate it with VO+Space.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if I want to look at the full workflow run instead of just the pull request summary?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the repository navigation and open the Actions tab. It is in the repo's top navigation, often near Projects and Security, with a play-button style icon. In the Actions tab, you can choose a workflow, then choose a run, then expand a job and read the step logs.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Logs are where the real clue usually lives.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You are looking for the first failing step, the error message, and any file names or line numbers. Some workflows also upload artifacts, which are files produced by the run, like test reports, coverage reports, screenshots, build output, or accessibility scan results.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What kinds of workflows should a new contributor expect to see in real projects?

speaker: ALEX
text: Continuous integration, or CI, is the big one. It usually means running tests every time someone opens or updates a pull request, so maintainers can see whether the change broke existing behavior.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then there are style checks, right? The ones that complain about formatting.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Linting checks code style and common mistakes. Documentation projects may run spelling checks, link checks, Markdown checks, or build the docs site to make sure the pages still compile.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Accessibility and security checks can show up too.

speaker: ALEX
text: They can. Accessibility workflows might scan pages for detectable issues, while security workflows might check dependencies or scan for known vulnerabilities. Deployment workflows are another common pattern: a project may deploy to production when code is pushed to main, or create a preview build for each pull request.

speaker: JAMIE
text: You mentioned reusable actions earlier. Where do maintainers find those?

speaker: ALEX
text: Many reusable actions are shared through the GitHub Marketplace under the Actions category. A maintainer can search for an action that sets up Node, checks out code, uploads an artifact, deploys a site, or runs a specific tool.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So an action is like a reusable automation component, not necessarily the whole workflow.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The workflow is the full recipe. An action is one reusable ingredient that a step can call with uses: and often configure with with: options.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about matrix builds? I see that phrase in a lot of CI files.

speaker: ALEX
text: A matrix build runs the same job across several combinations. For example, a project might test Node.js 18, 20, and 22, or test on ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, and macos-latest. That helps maintainers catch a problem that only appears in one version or one operating system.

speaker: JAMIE
text: For low vision learners, this is where indentation and nesting can get hard to track.

speaker: ALEX
text: Absolutely. Increase the editor font size, turn on visible whitespace in VS Code, and use YAML syntax highlighting if it helps. In workflow files, a line in the wrong indentation level can change the meaning or break the file entirely.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now, the moment everyone meets eventually: a check fails.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I appreciate naming that, because the first red X can feel like you broke the whole project.

speaker: ALEX
text: Usually you did not. Start by opening the failed check, then open the workflow run, then expand the failed job. Inside that job, find the step marked as failed and read the log around the error.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Should I read from the very top of the log?

speaker: ALEX
text: Not usually. Start near the failed step and look for the first real error message, not every warning. A useful error often mentions a command, a file path, a missing dependency, a test name, or a line number.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then I fix the issue locally or in the web editor, commit, and push again?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Pushing another commit to the same branch usually reruns the pull request checks. If you are stuck, leave a clear comment on the pull request that says which check failed, what error you found, and what you already tried.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That gives maintainers something concrete to respond to.

speaker: ALEX
text: Security matters a lot in workflows because automation can access code, tokens, and deployment systems.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Is that why GitHub sometimes asks maintainers to approve workflows from first-time contributors?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Some repositories require approval before running workflows on contributions from new or external contributors, especially when the workflow could use secrets or write permissions. That pause is a safety measure, not a personal rejection.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's define secrets, because that word is easy to misunderstand.

speaker: ALEX
text: A secret is an encrypted value stored in repository or organization settings, usually for API keys, tokens, passwords, or deployment credentials. Workflows can read secrets without printing the actual value, if they are configured correctly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And environment variables?

speaker: ALEX
text: Environment variables are named values available to commands while the job runs. Some are harmless, like a version number or a build mode. Sensitive values should be stored as secrets, not typed directly into a YAML file, a log, an issue, or a pull request comment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where does Dependabot fit into this?

speaker: ALEX
text: Dependabot can open pull requests that update dependencies or security alerts. Those PRs may trigger workflows too, and maintainers still review the checks before merging.

speaker: ALEX
text: Accessibility-focused workflows are helpful, but they are not magic.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Meaning they can catch some barriers automatically, but not every barrier a person might experience.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Tools such as GitHub's Accessibility Scanner Action, axe-based checks, pa11y, Lighthouse, or project-specific scripts can detect issues like missing labels, color contrast problems in some contexts, invalid HTML, and certain ARIA mistakes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: But they cannot tell whether the whole experience makes sense with a screen reader.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Automated scans do not replace keyboard testing, screen reader testing, magnification checks, plain language review, or feedback from disabled users. They are useful gates, but they are only part of accessibility practice.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Some workflows need the app running before they can scan it, yes?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. A workflow may need to install dependencies, build the project, start a local server, wait for the page to become available, and then point the scanner at that URL. On GitHub-hosted runners, the environment is temporary, so the workflow has to prepare everything it needs each time.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is a good hands-on activity for this appendix if I do not want to write a workflow from scratch?

speaker: ALEX
text: Pick a repository you are allowed to inspect and open.github/workflows. Choose one YAML file and identify its name, its on: triggers, the jobs it defines, the runner it uses, and one step that runs a command.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then I would open the Actions tab and compare the file to a real run.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Find a recent run, open a job, read several step names, and notice whether any artifacts were uploaded. If there is a pull request with checks, compare the PR status summary with the workflow run details.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the reflection questions are practical: What started the workflow? Which check would block a merge? Where would I click or activate if it failed? What would I tell a maintainer if I needed help?

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. GitHub Actions can look intimidating at first, but most contributor work comes down to reading the status, opening the failed run when needed, understanding the error, and making the next small fix.
